q: Under the provincial default, when is a school zone in effect on a school day?
why: Unless different municipal times are posted, Alberta school-zone periods are 8:00-9:30 a.m., 11:30 a.m.-1:30 p.m., and 3:00-4:30 p.m. on school days.

q: A school-zone sign displays times that differ from the provincial defaults. Which times apply?
a: The times posted on the sign
why: Municipalities may set different school-zone hours; posted times govern.

q: What is the school-zone speed limit in urban and rural Alberta unless otherwise posted?
why: The default school-zone maximum is 30 km/h when the zone is in effect.

q: You are behind a vehicle travelling 25 km/h in an active school zone. May you pass it?
a: Yes, if no children are present
No, passing in the same direction is prohibited while the zone is active
Only if the road has two lanes
why: Do not pass or attempt to pass another vehicle travelling in the same direction in an active school zone.

q: You see a school sign without an attached speed sign. What have you entered?
why: A school sign without a speed sign identifies a school area; use caution because children may be nearby.

q: Under the provincial default, when are playground-zone restrictions in effect?
a: Every day from 8:30 a.m. until one hour after sunset
why: Unless different times are posted, playground-zone restrictions apply every day from 8:30 a.m. until one hour after sunset.

q: At noon on a Sunday, you enter a playground zone with no special times posted. What maximum speed applies?
why: Playground zones apply every day during their effective hours, including Sundays, and are 30 km/h unless otherwise posted.

q: A playground sign has no speed-limit sign attached. What should you do?
a: Use caution because children may be nearby
Treat it as a school zone
why: The sign marks a playground area, not a speed zone, and warns drivers to use caution.

q: The pedestrian signal changes to DON'T WALK after someone has already begun crossing. What may the pedestrian do?
a: Wait for the next WALK signal in the roadway
why: A pedestrian who began crossing before DON'T WALK appeared may continue and clear the crosswalk.

q: You face a green arrow beside a red light. Which movement is allowed without stopping?
a: Only the direction shown by the arrow
No movement until all lights are green
why: A green arrow with a red light permits movement only in the arrow's direction.

q: All approaches at an intersection display flashing red lights. How should drivers treat it?
why: When every direction flashes red, the intersection operates as a four-way stop.

q: A flashing green light faces you. What should you remember even though opposing traffic faces red?
a: You must still yield to pedestrians and vehicles lawfully in the intersection
The signal is about to fail
why: A flashing green permits through or turning movements without stopping, but lawful intersection users still have priority.

q: How close must the wheels of a parallel-parked vehicle be to the curb?
why: The law requires the wheels to be no more than 50 centimetres from the curb.

q: Before beginning a parallel park, why should you brake gradually well before the space?
a: To alert following drivers with your brake lights
why: Early gradual braking slows the vehicle and warns drivers behind through the brake lights.

q: When first positioning beside the vehicle ahead of a parallel-parking space, about how much side clearance should you leave?
why: The guide recommends about one metre between the two vehicles before reversing.

q: Before pulling out from a parallel park, which blind-spot check is especially important?
a: Over the left shoulder for traffic and cyclists
Over the right shoulder for the curb
why: Check mirrors and look over the left shoulder for traffic and cyclists not visible in the mirrors.

q: Before opening the driver's door of a curbside parked vehicle, what should you check for?
a: Traffic and cyclists approaching from behind
why: Check mirrors and the left blind spot for approaching traffic or cyclists before opening the door.

q: From which direction should you approach a vehicle parked parallel to the curb before entering it?
a: From the traffic lane side only
why: Approach from the front so you can see traffic in the nearest lane before opening the door.

q: When entering a right-side angle-parking space, about how far should you travel from the parked vehicles?
why: The guide recommends staying about 1.5 metres from the rear of the parked vehicles.

q: While leaving an angle-parking stall, who has the right-of-way?
a: Traffic and pedestrians behind the parked vehicle
why: A driver backing from a parking stall must yield to traffic and pedestrians.

q: A vehicle beside you blocks your view while you reverse from an angle stall. What should you do?
a: Reverse quickly through the blind area
Move slowly, stop when needed, and check once you can see past it
Honk and assume others will stop
Turn immediately into the travel lane
why: Reverse slowly and be prepared to stop until you can see traffic and pedestrians beyond the obstructing vehicle.

q: Where may you enter a perpendicular or angle stall located to your left?
why: The guide says to enter a left-side perpendicular or angle stall only in a parking lot.

q: Why is a left-side 90-degree parking stall often easier to enter than a right-side stall?
a: It has a wider painted space
There is more room to achieve the proper turning angle
The steering wheel turns farther left
why: Approaching from the opposite side of the aisle provides more room to establish the proper angle, but oncoming traffic must be checked.

q: You technically have right-of-way, but another driver is not yielding. What should you do?
a: Do everything possible to prevent a collision
why: Right-of-way rules do not remove your responsibility to prevent a collision.

q: A peace officer directs you to stop while your traffic light is green. Which instruction controls?
why: Directions from a peace or police officer take priority over signs and signals.

q: With no stop line or marked crosswalk, how close to the intersecting roadway must you stop?
why: Stop within three metres of the intersecting roadway without interfering with pedestrians.

q: You approach a yield sign and see no traffic or pedestrians requiring you to yield. Must you stop?
a: No, you may proceed cautiously without a complete stop
Only if another vehicle is behind you
why: A yield sign requires slowing and yielding as needed, but not a stop when the way is clear.

q: At an uncontrolled T-intersection, does the vehicle travelling straight automatically have right-of-way?
a: No; the vehicle on the right has right-of-way
why: At an uncontrolled T-intersection, the normal rule still applies: yield to the vehicle on your right.

q: When leaving an alley across a sidewalk, where must you stop first?
a: Only if a pedestrian is visible
why: When exiting an alley, driveway, parking lot, or service road, stop before crossing the sidewalk and yield to pedestrians.

q: Do right-of-way rules apply at unmarked intersections in parking lots?
a: Only when a security guard is present
why: Parking lots contain uncontrolled intersections where normal right-of-way rules apply.

q: A vehicle ahead has stopped at an unmarked crosswalk for a pedestrian. May you pass it?
a: Yes, if the other lane is clear
No, do not pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian
why: Every intersection has marked or unmarked crosswalks, and you must not pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian.

q: In which direction does traffic circulate around an Alberta roundabout's centre island?
a: The direction shown by the nearest vehicle
why: Traffic circulates counterclockwise around the centre island.

q: When should you activate the right signal to take a later exit from a roundabout?
a: After passing the exit immediately before yours
why: Signal right after passing the exit before the one you intend to use.

q: You plan to take the first exit from a two-lane roundabout. Which approach lane should you use?
why: Approach in the right lane, stay right in the circle, and exit into the right lane.

q: You plan to travel past the first exit of a two-lane roundabout. Which lane should you generally use?
a: Any lane followed by a lane change inside
why: Drivers travelling past the first exit should use the left lane and remain in it through the circle.

q: While in a two-lane roundabout, you realize you cannot exit safely. What should you do?
a: Continue around in your lane and try again
why: Do not stop or cut across lanes; remain in your lane and travel around again.

q: You are exiting from the left lane of a roundabout. What must you check immediately before crossing the outside lane?
a: Traffic in the right lane continuing around
Only traffic behind the centre island
why: Check for vehicles in the right lane that may continue around before crossing that lane to exit.

q: How far in advance should you normally be established in the proper turning lane?
why: The guide recommends being in the proper turning lane at least 15 metres before the intersection.

q: Before turning right, why should you check over your right shoulder?
a: To detect cyclists and pedestrians approaching the intersection
To check the rear licence plate
To see whether the curb is painted
why: A right shoulder check helps detect cyclists and pedestrians in the curb-side blind area.

q: A parked vehicle is close to the corner in the curb lane you would normally enter. Where should you turn?
a: Behind the parked vehicle regardless of space
Into the first available lane left of the obstruction after yielding
why: When an obstruction is close to the corner, turn into the first available lane to its left and yield to traffic already using that lane.

q: You must wait in an intersection before completing a left turn. How should your front wheels be positioned?
why: Keep the wheels straight so a rear impact does not push the vehicle into oncoming traffic.

q: Before turning left from a two-lane highway, which extra check is important?
a: A left shoulder check for a vehicle passing you
A right shoulder check for parked cars
why: Check over the left shoulder to ensure another vehicle is not passing on your left.

q: Turning left from a two-way road onto a one-way road, which lane should you enter?
a: The first available lane on the left
why: Turn from the lane nearest the yellow line into the first available lane on the left side of the one-way road.

q: Turning left from a one-way road onto a two-way road, which lane should you enter?
a: The nearest lane to the right of the yellow line
why: Turn from the left lane into the nearest lane to the right of the yellow centre line.

q: When are dual-lane turns permitted?
a: Only where signs or pavement markings indicate them
why: Dual-lane turns may be made only where signs or pavement markings designate them.

q: While making a marked dual-lane turn, may you change lanes in the intersection?
a: No, stay in the corresponding lane
Only if the other vehicle slows
why: Maintain the corresponding lane throughout a dual turn; another vehicle may be turning beside you.

q: When should you enter a shared two-way left-turn lane?
a: Close to where you intend to turn
why: Enter the shared centre lane only near the point where you will turn left.

q: May you make a U-turn at a signal-controlled intersection without a sign specifically permitting it?
why: A U-turn at a signal-controlled intersection is prohibited unless a traffic-control device permits it.

q: In an urban area, may you make a U-turn at an alley intersection?
a: Only if no traffic is present
why: Urban U-turns are prohibited at alley intersections.

q: On a rural road near a hill crest, when is a U-turn prohibited?
a: When another driver within 150 metres cannot see you approaching from either direction
Only when the speed limit exceeds 80 km/h
Only when a centre line is present
why: Near a rural hill crest, a U-turn is prohibited where another approaching driver within 150 metres cannot see you.
